missionMode.title: Inbox Rescue: Urgency Attack
missionMode.brief: You have 60 seconds before close of day. Choose the safest response at each stage.

steps.prompt: An email says your account will be suspended in 30 minutes unless you verify via link. First move?

choices.label: Click immediately to avoid lockout
Pause and inspect sender/link details
Forward to team chat for opinions

steps.bestAction: Pause first. Urgency is the tactic. Check domain and message context before taking any action.

steps.prompt: The sender domain is close but not exact, and the email says not to contact IT. What next?

choices.label: Use the link but change password later
Reply asking for a 24-hour extension
Ignore email links and contact IT via known channel

steps.bestAction: Use a trusted channel you already know. Never trust contact paths provided by suspicious emails.

steps.prompt: You confirmed it's phishing. Final action?

choices.label: Delete it and move on
Report through official phishing process
Warn only your closest colleagues

steps.bestAction: Report quickly so IT can block the campaign and protect others.

moduleHero.title: Urgency is a social-engineering weapon
moduleHero.description: Attackers manufacture deadlines so you skip normal checks. Slow down, verify, then act.

redFlagSpotter.title: Spot the red flag
redFlagSpotter.prompt: You receive: 'Your Microsoft 365 account will be suspended in 30 minutes. Verify now at m365-security-check.co.' Which elements are phishing red flags?

flags.label: Threat of account suspension to force action

redFlagSpotter.explanation: Urgency attacks combine pressure + threat + untrusted link destinations. Product names alone are not proof of legitimacy.

quickTakeaway.title: 1-minute takeaway
points: Urgency is the trick — slowing down defeats it.
Never click links in time-pressured emails. Navigate directly instead.
Real IT issues almost never require immediate action via an email link.

microScenario.title: Quick decision check
microScenario.question: You get an email at 4:45 PM saying your Microsoft 365 account will be suspended in 30 minutes unless you verify your credentials. What do you do?

choices.label: Click the verification link — you can't afford to lose access
Reply to the email asking for more time
Ignore the link and contact IT directly to check your account status

microScenario.bestAction: Correct move: ignore the link and contact IT through a channel you already trust. Real account issues can always be resolved through IT — urgency in an email is a tactic, not a fact.

story.title: The tax-season email that exposed 12,000 employees
story.meta: Urgency · W-2 phishing · CEO impersonation · Seagate 2016
story.text:
Setup: During 2016 tax season, an HR employee at Seagate received an email that appeared to come from the CEO requesting W-2 records immediately. The timing made the request feel routine and urgent.

Attack: The employee replied with the data, trusting the apparent executive sender and deadline pressure. No malware was needed - just a convincing message at the right moment.

Impact: About 12,000 employee tax records were exposed and fraudulent filings followed. Seagate later settled a class-action lawsuit for $5.75 million.

Lesson: If a request involves sensitive data and urgency, verify through a trusted second channel before sending anything.
signals: Executive sender used to justify bypassing normal HR verification
Immediate deadline attached to a high-risk data request
Sensitive tax records requested over email rather than approved workflow

urgency.summary: Phishing doesn't rely on fancy hacking tools — it relies on you. Urgency is one of the most common tricks attackers use. By creating false time pressure, they push you into acting quickly without thinking. The goal is simple: make you panic so you skip the checks you'd normally do.
redFlags: Sudden, unexplained deadlines — "act within 30 minutes" or "respond immediately"
Threats of account closure, service interruption, or losing access to a tool
Requests to skip your normal steps — "don't go through IT, just click here"
Poor grammar, odd phrasing, or formatting that feels slightly off
Links where the destination address doesn't match the company it claims to be from — hover over any link before clicking to check where it actually goes
responseSteps: Stop and breathe — urgency is the trick, so slowing down defeats it
Do not click any links in the message
Open a new browser tab and navigate directly to the official site or tool yourself
If the email claims to be from IT or a known system, contact that person through a method you already trust — not anything provided in the email
Report the email using your organization's phishing report button or process

deeperLearning.title: Why urgency works on everyone — even careful people
points: When we feel rushed, the part of our brain that evaluates risk takes a back seat. This is a normal human response — not a personal failing.
Attackers deliberately manufacture urgency because they know it works consistently. A real IT issue or system outage almost never requires you to act within minutes via a link in an email.
A useful rule of thumb: the more urgent an email feels, the more carefully you should slow down and verify it. Legitimate organizations always give you time to check.

checkIn.question: You receive an email saying your account will be locked in 15 minutes. What is the first thing you should do?

choices.label: Click the link in the email to secure your account
Slow down, ignore the link, and navigate directly to the official site yourself
Reply to the sender to ask for more time
Forward it to a colleague to check

checkIn.explanation: Urgency is the manipulation tactic. Slowing down defeats it. Always navigate directly rather than following email links.

checkIn.question: A legitimate organization will typically allow you time to verify a request before acting.

choices.label: True — real organizations don't pressure you into acting in minutes
False — urgent requests are always genuine

checkIn.explanation: Real IT issues and account problems almost never require you to act within minutes via an email link. Artificial urgency is a hallmark of phishing.

quickTakeaway.title: 1-minute takeaway
points: Fear is designed to stop you verifying — recognise it as a warning sign, not a reason to act.
Real HR and legal notices never demand instant action via an email link.
If an email makes you anxious, pause. That feeling is exactly what the attacker is counting on.

microScenario.title: Quick decision check
microScenario.question: An email with your company's HR logo says your employment record has a compliance issue that could affect your contract, and you must resolve it by clicking a secure link within the hour. What do you do?

choices.label: Click the link immediately — you can't risk a contract issue
Reply to the email to ask what the compliance issue is
Contact HR directly through your normal channels to verify the issue exists

microScenario.bestAction: Correct move: contact HR through a channel you already trust. Real employment issues are handled through official processes — not one-hour deadlines delivered by email link.

story.title: The deepfake CFO call that triggered $25 million in transfers
story.text:
Setup: In 2024, a finance employee at Arup received a message about a confidential, urgent transaction from someone claiming to be the CFO. The employee had doubts at first.

Attack: A follow-up video call appeared to show the CFO and known colleagues giving direct instructions to proceed. The participants were AI deepfakes designed to create social pressure and make refusal feel risky.

Impact: The employee completed 15 wire transfers totaling HK$200 million (about US$25.6 million) to attacker-controlled accounts. The fraud was discovered only after head office confirmed no such transaction existed.

Lesson: Even voice and video confirmation can be faked - high-stakes requests still require independent verification through trusted channels.
signals: Confidential + urgent framing used to suppress normal challenge
Pressure from apparent leadership consensus to act immediately
Large transfer request proceeded without independent callback verification

intimidation.summary: Intimidation phishing uses fear to shut down your instinct to ask questions. By threatening legal consequences, disciplinary action, or account termination, attackers try to make you feel like you have no choice but to comply immediately. Nobody wants to get in trouble — and attackers exploit exactly that feeling.
redFlags: Scare tactics and a harsh, accusatory tone — language designed to make you feel at fault before you've done anything
Mentions of law enforcement, legal escalation, HR involvement, or "account termination"
Pressure to act without verifying — "do not contact IT, handle this immediately"
A sender address that doesn't match the organization it claims to represent
Vague accusations with no specific details — real HR or legal notices always include reference numbers and proper contact information
responseSteps: Don't react in fear — take a moment before doing anything at all
Never enter your credentials or personal information just because a message threatened you
Verify the claim independently by contacting HR, IT, or your manager using contact details you already know — not anything from the email
Remember: legitimate notices from HR or your legal team always involve proper context, reference numbers, and official channels
Report the message through your organization's phishing reporting process

deeperLearning.title: Fear overrides good judgment — by design
points: Intimidation phishing is specifically engineered to override your instinct to verify. When we're afraid of consequences, we tend to comply first and ask questions later — attackers count on this.
A real disciplinary or legal notice from your organization will never demand immediate action through an email link. It will involve your manager, HR, or formal written correspondence.
If an email makes you feel anxious or afraid, treat that emotional reaction as a warning sign — not a reason to act faster.

checkIn.question: An email threatens legal action unless you immediately provide your login credentials. What should you do?

choices.label: Provide the credentials to avoid consequences
Ignore the threat and verify the claim through official channels
Reply to ask what the legal action involves
Change your password using the link in the email

checkIn.explanation: Fear is designed to bypass your judgment. Real legal or HR notices include reference numbers and proper channels — never demand credentials via email.

checkIn.question: What is the main goal of intimidation tactics in phishing?

choices.label: To make the email look more official
To stop you from pausing to verify the request
To test whether you read emails carefully
To collect your name and job title

checkIn.explanation: Intimidation works by overriding your instinct to verify. When you're scared of consequences, you comply first — attackers count on that.

moduleHero.title: Fear is the payload
moduleHero.description: If a message makes you anxious or guilty, treat that emotion as a warning signal and verify off-channel.

redFlagSpotter.title: Spot the red flag
redFlagSpotter.prompt: An email says: 'Legal escalation has started due to your non-compliance. Submit credentials now to avoid HR action.' What should you flag?

flags.label: Demand for credentials in email flow

redFlagSpotter.explanation: Real legal or HR processes provide context, references, and official channels. Threat-only messaging is a classic intimidation pattern.

moduleHero.title: Scarcity triggers FOMO
moduleHero.description: Limited-time rewards are designed to rush judgment. Verify through trusted internal channels first.

redFlagSpotter.title: Spot the red flag
redFlagSpotter.prompt: Message: 'Only first 20 employees get a $150 voucher. Claim before 12:00 at company-benefits-claim.net.' Which cues are suspicious?

flags.label: Hard cutoff time to force speed

redFlagSpotter.explanation: Scarcity phishing relies on urgency + reward framing + external links. A specific reward value can still be fake.

quickTakeaway.title: 1-minute takeaway
points: If an email says 'limited spots' or 'expires today', treat it as a pressure tactic first.
Do not claim offers from email links. Verify in official internal channels.
Your goal is simple: pause, verify, then decide.

microScenario.title: Quick decision check
microScenario.question: It's 11:40 AM. You get an email saying only the first 20 employees get a wellness voucher if they "verify details" before lunch. What do you do next?

choices.label: Click immediately so you don't miss out
Forward it to your team so they can benefit too
Pause and verify via HR portal/internal comms before doing anything

microScenario.bestAction: Correct move: pause and verify through HR or official internal comms. Scarcity language is there to rush your judgment.

story.title: The open-enrollment lure that opened payroll access
story.meta: Scarcity · HR phishing · Benefits fraud · Documented campaign 2023–2024
story.text:
Setup: Open enrollment creates a real deadline each year, so benefit-related emails already feel time-sensitive. Attackers use that calendar pressure to make fake HR messages look believable.

Attack: In campaigns documented across 2023-2024, emails and QR codes pushed employees to "act before the deadline" and sign in to lookalike Microsoft 365 or HR portals. The urgency framed verification as a delay people could not afford.

Impact: Stolen credentials gave attackers access to payroll and benefits systems, enabling paycheck redirection, reimbursement fraud, and in some cases broader network compromise.

Lesson: If a reward or benefits deadline is driving your decision, stop and verify in the official HR portal - not through the email link or QR code.
signals: First-come or deadline language tied to login action
Email links or QR codes redirecting to lookalike sign-in pages
Benefits urgency used to bypass standard HR portal navigation

scarcity.summary: Scarcity phishing is built to make you act before you think. The message sounds exciting: limited offer, exclusive reward, first-come-first-served. The real objective is simple: rush you into clicking a link or sharing information before you verify anything.
redFlags: A countdown or deadline attached to a link: "claim by noon" or "expires today"
Reward language that feels unusually generous or out of pattern
A request to log in, verify, or submit details to unlock the offer
Sender domain that doesn't match the brand or company it claims to be
Generic targeting like "Dear Employee" instead of normal internal context
responseSteps: Pause for 10 seconds. Scarcity pressure loses power when you slow down.
Ask: Was I expecting this? Is this how HR or rewards are normally announced here?
Inspect the sender domain, not just the display name.
If it might be real, verify through your HR portal or trusted internal channel — never the email link.
Report suspicious reward emails so others don't get caught by the same lure.

deeperLearning.title: Why scarcity works so well
points: FOMO shortcuts good judgment. You stop verifying because you don't want to miss out.
Attackers know this and intentionally combine rewards + deadlines to force fast decisions.
Simple rule: if an email makes you feel hurried to get something valuable, verify first and click later.

checkIn.question: An email says you're one of only 50 employees to receive a $150 reward — click now before it expires. What do you do?

choices.label: Click immediately so you don't miss out
Verify through the HR portal or official internal communications first
Forward to colleagues so they can claim it too
Click but don't enter any personal information

checkIn.explanation: Scarcity + reward language is designed to trigger FOMO. Verify through official channels before taking any action.

checkIn.question: Which of these is a scarcity-based red flag?

choices.label: An email with a clear sender address from your organization
An email offering a limited-time reward from a domain like 'companyrewards25.biz'
An official announcement posted on the company intranet
An email from HR confirming your next training date

checkIn.explanation: Limited-time reward language plus an unfamiliar domain is a classic scarcity phishing pattern.

quickTakeaway.title: 1-minute takeaway
points: Authority pressure is meant to stop you from verifying.
High-stakes requests always need a second-channel check.
No real leader asks you to bypass controls.

microScenario.title: Quick decision check
microScenario.question: You get an email from a senior leader asking for an urgent payment outside process and saying to keep it confidential. What do you do first?

choices.label: Action it immediately to avoid delay
Reply and ask for more details in the same email thread
Verify through a trusted separate channel and follow normal approvals

microScenario.bestAction: Correct move: verify through a known channel and keep normal approval controls in place.

story.title: The CEO impersonation that cost €32 million
story.meta: Authority · BEC · CEO fraud · FACC AG 2016
story.text:
Setup: In 2016, a finance employee at FACC AG received an email appearing to come from the CEO requesting an urgent transfer for a confidential acquisition. The message looked credible and carried executive authority.

Attack: The employee was pressured to act quickly and quietly, without normal escalation. A single email request was treated as sufficient approval for a high-value transfer.

Impact: €42 million was sent to attacker-controlled accounts; about €10.9 million was recovered, leaving roughly €32 million lost. The incident also led to major leadership fallout and public market impact.

Lesson: Executive names do not override controls - any high-stakes payment request must be verified and approved through standard process.
signals: Senior identity used to force compliance with unusual payment request
Secrecy and urgency used to bypass dual-authorization controls
High-value transfer approved from email-only instruction

authority.summary: Authority phishing tries to make you obey first and think later. The message appears to come from someone senior and asks for urgent action — often money, credentials, or process exceptions. The attack works when pressure replaces verification.
redFlags: A senior-name sender asking for unusual financial or credential actions
Pressure to keep the request quiet or bypass normal approvals
Urgent language with no proper context or business reference
Sender address that is close to, but not exactly, your real domain
Tone that discourages questions: "Do this now, no delays"
responseSteps: Pause. Treat authority + urgency as a risk signal, not a command.
Verify the request through a channel you already trust (known phone/Teams contact).
Keep normal approvals in place — especially for payments and account changes.
Never send credentials, gift cards, or wire transfers from email-only requests.
Report authority-themed phishing attempts so finance and leadership can be alerted.

deeperLearning.title: Why authority attacks work
points: Most people are trained to respond quickly to leadership requests. Attackers exploit that reflex.
BEC succeeds when trust replaces process — not because people are careless.
Best rule: the higher the stakes, the stronger the verification requirement.

checkIn.question: Your CFO emails asking you to urgently buy gift cards and send the codes, keeping it secret from normal channels. What is the right response?

choices.label: Purchase the cards — questioning the CFO could be embarrassing
Verify by contacting the CFO directly through a method you already trust
Reply to the email asking for a purchase order number
Buy the cards and notify finance after

checkIn.explanation: Authority pressure is the tactic here. Verify through a separate known channel before acting.

checkIn.question: PAC leadership or IT will never ask you to do which of the following via email?

choices.label: Reset your password after you requested a reset
Click a link to join a scheduled meeting
Purchase gift cards or wire money without a formal approval process
Review a document shared on the company's approved system

checkIn.explanation: Anything that bypasses normal financial controls is a red flag, regardless of who appears to be asking.

moduleHero.title: Authority should never bypass process
moduleHero.description: Executive names can be spoofed. High-stakes requests always require second-channel verification.

types-of-phishing.summary: Phishing comes in many forms — attackers use as many methods as possible to reach you. Each type works a little differently, but they all share the same goal: get you to click, share, or act in a way that puts your information or your organization at risk. You don't need to memorize all of this — just knowing these methods exist makes you significantly harder to fool.

deeperLearning.title: When in doubt, always ask — that's how we all stay safe
points: You don't need to memorize every attack type. What matters is developing the habit of pausing before you click, call back, or hand over any information.
If something feels off — even just slightly — it is always okay to check with IT or your manager before taking action. No legitimate request will ever punish you for verifying.
Attackers rely on people staying silent and not asking questions. Speaking up is one of the most effective defenses we have as an organization.

types.description: Fake emails sent to large numbers of people, designed to look like they come from a trusted source — a bank, Microsoft, your IT team, or a delivery service. They contain malicious links or attachments. The goal is volume: send enough emails and someone will click.
signals: Generic greetings like "Dear User" or "Dear Customer" — no use of your actual name
Sender address with subtle misspellings (e.g. support@micr0soft.com)
Links or attachments you weren't expecting
Urgent or threatening language pushing you to act immediately

types.description: A targeted version of phishing that uses your name, your role, or real context from your work to appear legitimate. These are specifically crafted for you or your team, which makes them much harder to recognize than generic phishing emails.
signals: Uses your name or references a real project, but the request still feels unusual
Sender domain doesn't quite match the organization it claims to be from
Context that feels slightly "off" — overly specific in a strange way, or a topic you'd expect from someone else
Requests for credentials, files, or financial actions that seem out of the ordinary

types.description: Phishing via text message. Attackers send texts pretending to be from delivery companies, banks, or IT support to get you to tap a link on your phone. Because texts feel more personal and immediate than emails, they can be surprisingly convincing.
signals: Short, unrecognizable links — you can't see where they lead before tapping
Unsolicited messages about deliveries, banking alerts, or account issues you didn't initiate
Requests for personal information, passwords, or one-time codes via text
Messages from numbers you don't recognize, often with urgent language

types.description: Phishing over the phone. Attackers call pretending to be IT support, Microsoft, your bank, or even HR. They claim there's a virus on your computer, suspicious activity on your account, or an urgent issue requiring your credentials or remote access.
signals: Caller asks for your password, credentials, or to install software that gives them remote access to your computer
Pressure to act immediately — "we need to resolve this right now"
Unfamiliar or spoofed caller ID made to look official
Requests that your real IT or support team would never make over an unsolicited phone call

types.description: Attackers embed malicious URLs inside QR codes placed in emails, printed flyers, or even physical signage. Most people scan without seeing where the code leads first — which is exactly what makes this a growing threat that's easy to overlook.
signals: QR codes in unexpected emails asking you to log in, verify your identity, or claim something
Codes on printed materials in public spaces asking for personal or account information
No preview of the destination URL before you're taken to the site
Use a scanner app that previews the URL before opening — if the address looks unfamiliar or suspicious, don't proceed

checkIn.question: You receive a text message about a failed delivery with a short link to 'reschedule.' You weren't expecting a package. This is most likely:

choices.label: Spear phishing — targeted email using personal details
Smishing — phishing via SMS
Vishing — voice phishing
Quishing — QR code phishing

checkIn.explanation: Smishing is phishing delivered via text message. Unexpected delivery texts with short links are one of the most common smishing formats.

checkIn.question: Which phishing type uses personal information to appear credible to a specific target?

choices.label: Generic phishing — mass emails with no personalization
Spear phishing — targeted and personalized attacks
Quishing — QR code-based attacks
Smishing — SMS-based attacks

checkIn.explanation: Spear phishing uses real context — your name, role, colleagues, or current projects — to appear legitimate. This makes it much harder to spot than generic phishing.
